content:
I'm looking at some side project that needs to touch isFlasque for sheaves on a space with values in a general category C, and the current definition in mathlib is, in my opinion, wrong.

Currently the definition is that restriction maps are epimorphisms, but this doesn't even recover the intended notion for sheaves of rings. The Sierpinski space where the two assignments are Z (global sections) and Q (sections over the open point), and the restriction is the inclusion is an epi, but not surjective.

Claude suggested the following example: take the poset {p < a > q} and the resulting finite topology coming from it (so proper opens {p,a}, {q,a}, {a}) , and k a field. The sheaf of rings with sections k[x] at {p,a} and {q,a}, and k(x) at {a}, with the restriction maps the inclusions is flasque by the mathlib definition, but allegedly has non-vanishing cohomology H^1 = k(x)/k[x] (calculated in Ab). This space is even (it seems) contractible, so all constant-coefficient cohomology vanishes.

I'd like to propose:

class IsFlasque : Prop where
  strongEpi : ∀ {U V : (Opens X)ᵒᵖ} (i : U ⟶ V), StrongEpi (F.map i)

Mathlib has CategoryTheory.StrongEpi and good API to recover the API that holds for the current definition of isFlasque using just CategoryTheory.Epi

For abelian categories, toposes, categories of algebraic things (something like concrete with monadic underlying set functor) I think this reduces to the existing definition, though this might need some scaffolding. I think that existing headline theorems in mathlib for flasque sheaves will still work and even generalise away from abelian categories, to say Barr-exact (or, with care, regular categories) so that they work for semiabelian category-valued sheaves for non-abelian cohomology.

Before I start the quest to get a mathlib PR up, I'd like to hear people's thoughts.
cc @Raphael Douglas Giles and @Brian Nugent (hope that's the right one) as you had two theorems committed to mathlib that would need re-doing this year (mathlib4#38775 and mathlib4#35785 resp.)

I don't understand your example: You are checking if the sheaf is flasque as a sheaf of rings, but then compute its cohomology as a sheaf of abelian groups. Should you not also check "flasque"ness as a sheaf of abelian groups in that case? Then the maps are no longer epi's and everything is in order, no?

I agree the example is not a strong one, and I debated including it. I don't think that it's really needed to appreciate my point. (as I said, Claude suggested it, I was also a bit dubious about the quotient calculated in Ab not Ring, but there you go: ignore it if you wish)

The theorems currently in mathlib could work for sheaves valued in semiabelian categories, for instance. thus sheaves of nonabelian groups hence you can get some nonabelian cohomology results in the low degrees where these exist.

I think the (imho better) new definition allows for better use-cases outside just abelian category- and Set-valued sheaves.

That is to say, this feels like mathlib-style "good generality", whereas category theoretically, the current definition with just plain epimorphisms feels unmotivated, and only "justified" by examples where many notions of epimorphisms have collapsed into a priori stronger definitions.
Do you have a reference for this definition of flasque sheaves?

No, it's based on trying to make sure the theorems work for more categories than is currently stated. A strong epi is a very slight strengthening (no pun intended) of the notion of vanilla epimorphism, and for all the applications currently stated it holds for them. For categories of algebras for a Lawvere theory (which are regular), strong = regular, for instance, and these are the epimorphisms surjective on underlying sets.

If you want something, then Hartshorne II Ex. 1.16 defines a flasque sheaf (no specified category in which the sheaves are valued) to be one where the restriction maps are surjective, and unless one wants a sheaf of rings to have its own special notion of flasque, then the definition in mathlib with C=CommRing underspecifies what is needed. Generally in this chapter Hartshorne is sticking to sheaves of abelian groups but explicitly says

.... let the reader make the necessary modifications for the case of rings, sets, etc.

I'm happy to go away and formalise everything and come back with receipts, if that is wanted, but if there are justified mathematical or formalisation reasons why the current definition is the mathlib-generality correct one, I wanted to know so as to not waste my time.

And by formalise-to-get-receipts I confess I mean ask Claude to switch out the definitions and patch the proofs, which at this point I think is only light surgery. I very much know is not mathlib-suitable. It would be just be a proof of concept to show nothing breaks and more theorems are available for proper formalisation.

If you are willing to countenance a sheaf of commutative monoids (perhaps a better example than that of rings), then N -> Z (both additive) is an epi in the category of comm. monoids, but not surjective. Would a sheaf with such a restriction map be counted as flasque?

I do not think there is any need to change the definition. The only application of flasque sheaves that I know of are related to cohomology. Cohomology is defined using Ext-groups in categories of sheaves of abelian groups (even showing that we get the same cohomology groups by using Ext-groups in categories of sheaves of R-modules when it makes sense is not trivial).
We could have used the surjectivity of F(X) -> F(U) as the definition of flasque, but this would require assuming that the category is concrete. Using Epi was a good compromise as the API for it is sufficiently developed, it makes sense for any category and it is equivalent in the cases which are important (Type, Ab, ModuleCat R) for the cohomological applications.

If we want to be closer to the idea of "surjective on sections" without requiring concrete categories, wouldn't effective epimorphisms be a better pick than plain Epi?
iirc, for all "concrete algebraic categories", this is the notion that translates to "surjective on carriers*
"the only applications I personally can think of" is not good mathlib policy imho
Do you have references for other applications?
As I said, I'm happy to go off and vibe prove my proposal to show that nothing in mathlib breaks and then more theorems are available.
I'm thinking cohomology valued in crossed modules as a tentative target

But even then, aren't we pure mathematicians, and since when is a deciding factor "well, I think that because I can't imagine examples, we should stop and not ever think about how to better reframe this definition"?

Robin Carlier said:

If we want to be closer to the idea of "surjective on sections" without requiring concrete categories, wouldn't effective epimorphisms be a better pick than plain Epi?
iirc, for all "concrete algebraic categories", this is the notion that translates to "surjective on carriers*

For concrete algebraic categories at least three classes of epimorphism collapse, so picking any of them is reasonable. My view is that picking the weakest one from that class (weakest for other example categories) that still allows the theorems to go through with minimal effort is the right one

The definition in mathlib is already general enough as compared to the literature. The potential applications of a change in the definition seem very speculative to me. If the future proves me wrong, it would be an easy refactor anyway. In the meantime, discussing this does not seem to be the best use of anyone's time. (IMO, there are more important things to do with flasque sheaves!)
I am happy to refactor it now, is what I am saying, and have the api so that no change is apparent from any existing uses.

As it stands the definition is not even consistent with the literature for the case of models of a Lawvere theory in a sheaf topos on a space aka sheaves valued in algebras for that theory, because of the existence of epimorphisms that are non-surjective on the underlying functions.

I'm not saying to make the definition more general, I'm saying to tighten it in a way that changes nothing for existing mathlib uses, but doesn't leave the door open for examples that fail to meet the assumption in the literature about what flasqueness is.
The definition in mathlib seems to be consistent with what I can see in the last references mentionned at https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/flabby+sheaf

@Robin Carlier fwiw, for a category of algebras for a Lawvere theory, regular descent morphism = descent morphism = effective epi = regular epi = strict epi = strong epi = extremal epi = surjective on underlying sets, so one is spoiled for choice as to what class of epimorphisms one uses. As a default, for a generic category, the desideratum is to be closed under operations one needs, like composition, pullback, etc. and for classes like regular epi this doesn't hold always, so there is real content in choosing the class of epimorphisms appropriately.

Since no one is giving me technical lean reasons nor mathematical reasons other than "why bother?" or "I can't think of examples", I'll do the proof of concept and report back how minimal/easy the refactor is

@Joël Riou since those are either for a topos (Blechschmidt) T-algebras for a monad T on a topos (Kock) or in univalent mathematics (models are higher toposes) I will push back and say that this in no way justifies using plain epimorphisms for an arbitrary category, because in a topos the only distinction is between split epis and all other classes which collapse into one.
Wikipedia's definition is "surjective on underlying sets" which is stricter than mathlib in cases where that applies.
EoM only disusses it for sets with values in a concrete category, and is again the same as Wikipedia
Tamme only defines it for abelian sheaves (i.e. abelian group-valued sheaves), in terms of acyclicity of Cech cohomology.
Moreover the nLab itself is defining it for sheaves of sets, then implicitly for sheaves of abelian groups for one claim

David Michael Roberts said:

Since no one is giving me technical lean reasons nor mathematical reasons other than "why bother?" or "I can't think of examples"

Note that these are perfectly good reasons. Pursuing generality for its own sake is often a bad move, the definitions should be motivated by forthcoming examples and applications.

My contention is that mathlib has already fallen prey to early generality: why was the theorem stated for arbitrary categories C when it could have been stated for abelian categories, which are the use-cases I see and getting the gist of? Or for concrete categories?

Proving Flasque.of_shortExact_of_isFlasque₁₂ Flasque.epi_of_shortExact for sheaves with values in semiabelian categories not just for sheaves of abelian groups feels like a reasonable theorem, but of course I don't know what the overall grand plan is in this space, which is why I'm bringing this up.

David Michael Roberts said:

My contention is that mathlib has already fallen prey to early generality: why was the theorem stated for arbitrary categories C when it could have been stated for abelian categories, which are the use-cases I see and getting the gist of? Or for concrete categories?

It was stated for arbitrary categories as a formalization convenience, there isn’t anything in the definition that makes use of the added structure provided by an Abelian category.

Since the notion is only used when studying cohomology it seems fine to implicitly assume the category is abelian. At the start you say you are working on a project that requires flasque sheaves on general categories? Maybe it’s best if you do your project first then discuss a potential refactor. It’ll be more clear if there is a real reason for it if there’s an example of it being useful.
Is a theorem for C a regular category enough? (never mind, I won't push this further)
(deleted)

Apologies, that was ungenerous of me.

I will throw the current definition in the same bucket as "we need to define division as a total function, so division by 0 is defined as junk value we will never arrive at", which I don't mind being a fact of life. It's just not something I'd expect for a definition involving categories... ^_^

Just to close the loop, because I said it would do it, here is the diff for the proof of concept. Just to reiterate, I'm no longer arguing for this, it's merely the completionist urge in me.

Epi_to_StrongEpi_changes.txt
Thanks everyone for your patience and bearing with me.
Can someone mark this as resolved?
Joël Riou has marked this topic as resolved.
